questions.text: I routinely spend my free time on activities that benefit me personally.
I would decline an award or honor and redirect attention to the team.
I see my job as pointing the group in the right direction and clearing the path.
I feel empowered when the group trusts me enough to share power.
I naturally distribute decision-making power more broadly as projects progress.
When I learn that someone I know is going through a difficult time, my first instinct is to consider how I might help.
I notice when a person brings up old information at a strategic moment to shift the dynamics of a conversation.
I feel responsible for creating the conditions that will lead to my desired future.
Hearing that someone has had bad news usually doesn't make me want to reach out.
I rarely notice when someone is posturing for an audience during a meeting.
I notice that I can shift my attention away from emotional stimuli relatively easily.
I schedule specific times to check and respond to messages rather than staying reactive.
I do not naturally sense when two people are having a power struggle disguised as polite conversation.
My baseline state is one of such stability that disruptions feel like small departures rather than upheavals.
A person's hardship stops mattering to me soon after I hear about it.
I sense when a shared meal or coffee is actually a pretext for a conversation someone needs to have.
I routinely assess whether my current role still serves my personal growth trajectory.
I routinely bring extra food, supplies, or materials to share with whoever might need them.
I check and respond to messages whenever they arrive, staying in the flow of communication.
I notice when someone positions a request as a suggestion to make it more palatable.
When someone shares a painful experience, the fact of their pain carries little weight in my mind.
Someone's pain matters even more to me when they have no one else to turn to.
I often take it upon myself to resolve group disagreements by choosing a path.
I reconnect with people when the impulse strikes rather than tracking our last contact.
When I get good news, the euphoria can last for days.
I calibrate my effort to the importance of each task, giving more attention to high-impact work.
I tend to share my food, my space, and my belongings without a second thought.
I learn what I want to achieve by starting to act, not by planning in advance.
I routinely upgrade my personal environment—better lighting, better furniture, better technology.
I notice that my emotional reactions to the same type of event are remarkably consistent over time.
I tend to be focused on my own train of thought during conversations rather than scanning for reactions.
I am attracted to opportunities where I can set the tone for a team.
I wish I could relieve suffering I hear about, even when I have no means to.
After a heated exchange, my body stays in fight-or-flight mode long after the words have stopped.
I experience the first moments of waking up after a bad dream as indistinguishable from the terror of the dream itself.
I prefer that group deliverables be finalized by whoever the group entrusts with that task.
